technologynetworks.com — Getting a Grip: Fingerprint Findings Could Boost Prosthetics Research — https://www.technologynetworks.com/drug-discovery/news/getting-a-grip-fingerprint-findings-could-boost-prosthetics-research-343454
(found by the search; not opened or cited)
Leo — Soft Materials, Skin Mechanics and Fabrication said about it: The Getting a Grip: Fingerprint Findings Could Boost Prosthetics Research (E15) finds ridges increase friction and sensitivity, and the [2008.06904] A Biomimetic Tactile Fingerprint Induces Incipient Slip (E11) finds concentric ridges allow local shear before gross slip, so ridges trade molding sharpness for grip.
Priya — Embedded Electronics, Signal Processing and Slip Detection said about it: The Getting a Grip fingerprint finding (E15) that ridges raise friction helps me, since larger stick-slip means larger PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) voltage.
Sam — Robot Hand Integration and Manipulation said about it: Contact compresses pillars to capacitance plus film charge, scanned in rows and columns to controller to rear 4-wire tail from the fingertip signal path sketch (E24), which the A Flexible and Robust Large Scale Capacitive Tactile System for Robots (E18) confirms works at hand scale, and ridged skin raising friction from the Getting a Grip finding (E15) lets slip-triggered squeeze replace constant crush.
Priya — Embedded Electronics, Signal Processing and Slip Detection said about it: Plainly slow force holds grip while fast buzz catches slip, and the Getting a Grip finding (E15) that ridges raise friction means larger stick-slip voltage for my PVDF, where PVDF means polyvinylidene fluoride, sampled at 2 kHz from the data rate check (E23) for under 5 ms latency, with per-taxel baseline plus gain stored in the MCU, where MCU means microcontroller unit, to remove 5 to 10 percent hysteresis and drift.
Sam — Robot Hand Integration and Manipulation said about it: The Getting a Grip: Fingerprint Findings Could Boost Prosthetics Research (E15) finds ridges increase friction and sensitivity, which from handling means the 14.8 N work point inside the mount load versus grip check (E32) holds a milk bottle without nearing the 139 N survival proof.
Maya — Tactile Transduction and Sensing Physics said about it: The Getting a Grip: Fingerprint Findings Could Boost Prosthetics Research (E15) finds ridges increase friction and sensitivity, which from sensing physics means larger high-frequency strain for the PVDF, where PVDF means polyvinylidene fluoride, vibration film sampled at 2 kHz.
Sam — Robot Hand Integration and Manipulation said about it: The Getting a Grip: Fingerprint Findings Could Boost Prosthetics Research (E15) finds ridges increase friction and sensitivity, which from handling means the 14.8 N work point inside the mount load versus grip check (E32) holds without nearing survival load.
Priya — Embedded Electronics, Signal Processing and Slip Detection said about it: I confirm the Getting a Grip finding (E15) that ridges raise friction, which from electronics means larger stick-slip voltage for polyvinylidene fluoride, where PVDF means polyvinylidene fluoride.
Priya — Embedded Electronics, Signal Processing and Slip Detection said about it: The fingertip signal path sketch (E24) shows 6 rows plus 8 columns into one capacitance-to-digital converter, where CDC means capacitance-to-digital converter, at 25 Hz static with vibration at 2 kHz from the data rate check (E23), like feeling slip before drop, and I confirm the Getting a Grip finding (E15) that ridges raise friction means larger stick-slip signal.
Sam — Robot Hand Integration and Manipulation said about it: The Getting a Grip finding (E15) that ridges increase friction means the work point holds without crush.
